question: Which Australian marsupial is famous for producing droppings shaped like little cubes?
source_excerpt: Of all the poops in the world, only wombats' are shaped like cubes.

extra.why_interesting: Players assume nature never makes cubes, and certainly not from a digestive tract. Many have seen this fact go viral, and it is absurd enough to stick.
extra.verification_notes: Wombats are the only known animal producing cube-shaped droppings; no contradicting or newer information found (https://www.sciencenews.org/article/how-wombats-poop-cubes).

explanation: Different sections of the wombat's intestine stretch differently, and that sculpts the corners. The cubes stack neatly on rocks and logs, where they mark territory without rolling away.

question: Scotland's official national animal doesn't actually exist. What is it?
source_excerpt: The unicorn is Scotland's national animal, though it is a mythical creature rather than a real one.

extra.why_interesting: Players expect a real animal such as a stag, eagle or Highland cow. The real answer is a mythical creature, and once heard it feels oddly fitting.
extra.verification_notes: The unicorn is widely documented as Scotland's national animal and is mythical, so the pair stands; the 'official' wording is slightly loose, but no source contradicts it (https://www.nts.org.uk/stories/the-unicorn-scotlands-national-animal).

explanation: The unicorn stood for purity and power in Celtic mythology. It still appears in chains on the royal coat of arms, opposite England's lion.

question: In 1971, an Apollo 14 astronaut used a smuggled club head to hit two balls across the surface of the Moon. Which sport was he playing?
source_excerpt: Shepard's first ball angled off into a crater, while the second went up and away even though he was wearing a bulky spacesuit and backpack.

extra.why_interesting: Players picture strict science on the lunar surface, not leisure. The clue 'hit two balls' leaves only a few sports possible, so the answer can be reasoned out.
extra.verification_notes: Alan Shepard hit two golf balls on the Moon during Apollo 14 in 1971 with a smuggled six-iron head; no newer event changes this (https://www.ksat.com/sports/2021/02/05/out-of-this-world-shepard-puts-golf-on-moon-50-years-ago/).

explanation: Alan Shepard attached a six-iron head to a sample-collecting tool. Wearing a stiff spacesuit, he swung one-handed and joked that the ball went 'miles and miles'.

question: The Caesar salad has nothing to do with Rome. In which country was it actually invented?
source_excerpt: created on July 4, 1924, by restaurateur Caesar Cardini at his restaurant, Caesar's, in Tijuana, Mexico

extra.why_interesting: The name points to Julius Caesar and Italy, so most players say Italy. The real answer is just across the US border.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia reports Caesar Cardini invented the salad in 1924 at his Tijuana, Mexico restaurant, and the disputed claims (his brother Alex, staff such as Livio Santini) are also Tijuana-based.

explanation: Italian immigrant Caesar Cardini threw it together at his restaurant in Tijuana in the 1920s. Americans had crossed the border to dine and drink during Prohibition.

question: Counting its overseas territories, which country spans the most time zones, beating both Russia and the USA?
source_excerpt: France has the most time zones, including its overseas territories: 12 (13 counting its Antarctic claim). Russia and the United States each have 11.

extra.why_interesting: Players think of the giant countries first. Ruling out Russia and the USA forces them to think about scattered territories, and France then becomes reachable.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia's list of time zones by country gives France 12 (13 with Antarctic claim) versus 11 each for Russia and the USA.

explanation: French Polynesia, Réunion, New Caledonia and other islands stretch France across 12 time zones. That rises to 13 if you count its Antarctic claim.

question: Long before Mario, Nintendo was founded in Kyoto in 1889. What did it originally make?
source_excerpt: founded on 23 September 1889 in Shimogyō-ku, Kyoto, Japan, by craftsman Fusajiro Yamauchi... to produce and distribute Japanese playing cards, especially hanafuda

extra.why_interesting: Players link Nintendo only with consoles. The founding year of 1889 rules out anything electronic and pushes them towards a traditional game.
extra.verification_notes: Nintendo was founded in Kyoto in 1889 to make Japanese playing cards (hanafuda), per https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo.

explanation: Fusajiro Yamauchi set the company up to hand-make hanafuda, traditional Japanese flower cards. Nintendo still sells them today.

question: The first patent for a fax-style machine, which sent images down telegraph wires, was granted in which decade?
source_excerpt: Alexander Bain is credited with inventing the first fax machine patented in England in 1843.

extra.why_interesting: The fax feels like 1980s office tech, so players pick late decades. In fact it is older than the telephone, which arrived in 1876.
extra.verification_notes: Alexander Bain patented a facsimile-style telegraph in 1843 (1840s), consistent across sources; no later development changes this.

explanation: Alexander Bain patented his image-sending telegraph in 1843. That is more than 30 years before Bell's telephone.

question: How many hearts does an octopus have?
source_excerpt: octopuses have three hearts: one systemic heart and two branchial (gill) hearts

extra.why_interesting: This is a well-loved classic and an easy entry point. Players may half-remember 'more than one' and have to commit to a number.
extra.verification_notes: Octopuses have three hearts (one systemic, two branchial), confirmed by https://www.livescience.com/how-many-hearts-does-an-octopus-have; no newer finding contradicts it.

explanation: Two hearts pump blood through the gills and the third supplies the rest of the body. Their copper-based blood is blue.

question: Which is the only country whose national flag is not a rectangle?
source_excerpt: The flag of Nepal is the world's only national flag that isn't a quadrilateral.

extra.why_interesting: Players assume all flags are rectangles. Those who have seen this distinctive flag recall it instantly, and the Himalayan shape gives a mnemonic hook.
extra.verification_notes: Nepal's flag, made of two stacked pennons, is widely documented as the only non-quadrilateral national flag; square flags (Switzerland, Vatican) are still rectangles mathematically, and no newer change was found. https://www.montana.edu/everest/facts/flag-of-nepal.html

explanation: Nepal's flag is two stacked triangular pennants, often said to echo the Himalayan peaks. Its constitution even specifies the exact geometry for drawing it.

question: ABBA launched their global career by winning Eurovision in 1974. Which song, named after a famous battle, did they win with?
source_excerpt: Waterloo won the Eurovision Song Contest 1974, held at the Brighton Dome in Brighton, England, on 6 April 1974.

extra.why_interesting: This is an easy, joyful pop moment. The fun twist is that a Napoleonic defeat launched one of pop's greatest victories.
extra.verification_notes: ABBA won Eurovision 1974 with 'Waterloo', named after the Battle of Waterloo; no newer events affect this (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waterloo_(ABBA_song)).

explanation: 'Waterloo' won in Brighton in 1974 and made ABBA Sweden's first Eurovision champions. Napoleon's defeat became their breakthrough.

question: The marathon's oddly precise 42.195 km was fixed so the race could finish in front of the royal box. In which city were those 1908 Olympics held?
source_excerpt: The distance from the stadium entrance to the Royal Box was 385 yards. Olympedia puts the total at precisely 26 miles, 385 yards (42,195 metres).

extra.why_interesting: Players assume the strange distance comes from ancient Greece. In fact it was a royal convenience, and the 1908 date gives enough of a foothold to recall the host city.
extra.verification_notes: The 1908 Olympics were in London, and the 42.195 km distance came from the Windsor-to-royal-box course; see https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_1908_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Men%27s_marathon

explanation: The 1908 course ran from Windsor Castle to the royal box at White City Stadium. That awkward distance later became the official standard.

question: On hot summer days, the Eiffel Tower can grow up to about 15 centimetres taller. Why?
source_excerpt: engineers monitoring the monument find a real-world seasonal variation of 12 to 15 centimetres

extra.why_interesting: A building changing height sounds impossible, but everyday physics solves it. This gives the 'of course' moment.
extra.verification_notes: Thermal expansion of the tower's iron is the accepted explanation, and sources put the summer growth at roughly 5–15 cm, so 'up to about 15 cm' is acceptable (https://interestingengineering.com/culture/the-eiffel-tower-grow-taller-each-summer).

explanation: The tower is made of iron, which expands as it heats up. The side facing the sun swells most, so the top also leans slightly away from it.

question: Which popular nut grows dangling from the bottom of a fleshy fruit called an 'apple'?
source_excerpt: The cashew nut hangs from the base of the cashew apple, which is the fleshy part.

extra.why_interesting: Players picture nuts growing inside shells on branches. A nut dangling outside its fruit is bizarre, and there are few candidates for an 'apple' with a nut.
extra.verification_notes: The cashew nut hangs from the base of the fleshy cashew apple (a pseudofruit), per https://www.mentalfloss.com/article/31226/cashew-nuts-grow-out-crazy-apples; no newer development changes this.

explanation: Each cashew hangs beneath its own cashew apple, a juicy fruit eaten in Brazil and India. The nut's shell holds a caustic oil, which is why cashews are never sold in the shell.

question: Three of these Central European countries are landlocked. Which one has its own sea coast?
source_excerpt: Slovenia's coastline stretches approximately 47 km (29 mi) between Italy and Croatia.

extra.why_interesting: All four are similar Central European countries, and two of them are famously confused by name. Players have to actually know which one reaches the sea.
extra.verification_notes: Slovenia has a ~47 km Adriatic coastline while Hungary, Austria and Slovakia are landlocked (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geography_of_Slovenia).

explanation: Slovenia has a short strip of Adriatic coast, under 50 km long, with the port of Koper. The others have no sea coast at all.

question: Who is the only person ever to win Nobel Prizes in two different sciences?
source_excerpt: she was and still is the only person to be awarded Nobel Prizes in two scientific categories.

extra.why_interesting: Players know Curie as a pioneer, but the 'only person ever' record adds surprise. A motivated player gets there.
extra.verification_notes: Nobel Prize site confirms Curie (Physics 1903, Chemistry 1911) is the only person awarded in two scientific categories; no newer laureate has matched this (https://www.nobelprize.org/stories/women-who-changed-science/marie-curie/).

explanation: Curie won Physics in 1903 for research on radioactivity and Chemistry in 1911 for discovering polonium and radium. Over a century later, no one has matched her.

question: Which African country is home to more ancient pyramids than Egypt?
source_excerpt: Sudan has at least 230 (some posit up to 255) examples still standing

extra.why_interesting: Egypt owns the pyramid image in everyone's mind. Nubia as a neighbouring civilisation is the reasoning path, and Egypt's southern neighbour is guessable.
extra.verification_notes: Guinness World Records lists Sudan with at least 230 pyramids versus Egypt's roughly 120-140, so Sudan has more; I found no newer events that overturn this.

explanation: The kings of ancient Nubia built around 200 steep, narrow pyramids at sites like Meroë. That is more than Egypt has, though they are much smaller.

question: Which lake, the deepest on Earth at more than 1,600 metres, holds about a fifth of the world's unfrozen surface fresh water?

extra.why_interesting: Players guess the Great Lakes or Victoria, assuming that big area means most water. Depth is the hidden key.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia lists Baikal's maximum depth as 1,642 m, calls it the world's deepest lake, and gives about 19–23% of the world's fresh water, consistent with 'about a fifth'.

explanation: Siberia's Lake Baikal holds more water than all five North American Great Lakes combined. It is also around 25 million years old, the oldest lake on Earth.

question: Roughly how many trees are there on Earth?
source_excerpt: Study finds many, many more trees than previously estimated: about 3.04 trillion trees on Earth

extra.why_interesting: Players anchor on the 8 billion human population and undershoot. Realising there are hundreds of trees for every person is a delightful scale shock.

topicality.rationale: Ecology estimate, not tied to a news event.

extra.verification_notes: Crowther et al. (Nature 2015) estimated ~3.04 trillion trees; options differ by orders of magnitude so 3 trillion is the only defensible choice.

explanation: A 2015 study in Nature counted about 3 trillion trees, roughly 400 for every person alive. That is still around half the number before human civilisation began clearing forests.

question: On a hot summer day, the Eiffel Tower stands roughly 15 centimetres taller than it does in deep winter, and nobody adds a single bolt. What physical effect is responsible?
source_excerpt: The growth comes from thermal expansion: heated iron lengthens, and the tower's height changes with the seasons.

extra.why_interesting: Players picture a 330-metre iron landmark as completely fixed. Learning that it grows by the length of a pencil every summer is surprising, and the cause is something everyone has met in a stuck jar lid or a sagging power line.

topicality.rationale: Evergreen physics fact about thermal expansion, not tied to any news event.

extra.verification_notes: The Eiffel Tower grows roughly 12–15 cm in summer heat because of thermal expansion of its iron (https://interestingengineering.com/culture/the-eiffel-tower-grow-taller-each-summer).

explanation: Iron expands as it warms, and over about 300 metres of structure that adds up to around 15 centimetres. The sun also makes the top lean slightly away from whichever side is being heated.
